RagShortTexts: The economic sustenance of Goths in 374 AD relied upon extensive agrarian estates, pastoral herds, and strategic mineral extraction.
Anchored around commercial hubs near Lower Danube Floodplains, merchant caravans traded valuable bullion, grain, wine, and exotic raw goods.
Advanced weapon smithies and metallurgical workshops provided the industrial backbone necessary to equip large armies in the field.

Variants.Content: Underpinning the immense martial demands of Goths was an agrarian and mercantile economic system rooted in rural estates and municipal workshops. Across fertile valleys and pastures, countless tenant farmers and laborers produced wheat harvests, vintage wines, cured pelts, and high-grade iron ingots destined for storehouses. Within thriving market plazas around Lower Danube Floodplains, cosmopolitan merchants converged to barter gold coinage, imported silks, fine armaments, and livestock. Imperial or royal customs officials maintained toll gates, extracting heavy excise duties from freight wagons. Yet the system faced constant vulnerability from harvest failures and trade route disruptions, compelling rulers to enforce grain requisitions to sustain armies in the field.

Mud claims the axles of the supply wagons at the river ford, and the men heave them out one wheel at a time. The requisitioned rations are rock hard, and this month's pay came in salt and copper. A warrior keeps his eyes on the far bank and hopes the next skirmish will yield silver from a fallen rider's belt.

The bailiff balances the books by lamplight: the smithies sent off ninety horseshoes and forty spearheads, and the hide merchants at the river fair paid in advance. Those sales cover the mail for the household knights. He reminds the chamberlain that a late payment would leave the cavalry idle through the autumn.
